A science project built by Steve Jobs back when he was in the eighth grade has found a new owner after selling at a recent auction for $34,375. The late co-founder of Apple put the presentation together while attending Cupertino Junior High in 1968. The lot offered bidders a rare glimpse into the early technical interests of a teenager who would eventually change the computing landscape forever.

The plywood presentation board explains how a silicon rectifier works

The project is officially titled “What is the SCR?” and breaks down the mechanics of a silicon-controlled rectifier. It features a main display board built out of plywood and divided into three separate sections.

The left side holds a wooden model showing the different semiconductor layers. The center panel contains actual test circuits to demonstrate how the component functions in real life. Finally, the right side provides a detailed diagram of a 25-amp unit.

Along with the board, the winning bidder received a ten-page report dated February 29, 1968, and submitted to a teacher named Mrs. Yakel. The young student even left a handwritten note for the science fair judges. He instructed them to plug in specific circuits to an oscilloscope to see the device run, while politely asking them to unplug everything when finished.

His stepbrother kept the childhood item after offering it back

This piece of history made its way to the auction block through John Chovanec, the stepbrother of the tech icon. Chovanec’s mother married Paul Jobs in 1990. After Paul passed away in 1993, Chovanec reached out multiple times to see if his stepbrother wanted to collect his old personal items from the family home in Los Altos.

When Steve Jobs declined to pick up the belongings, Chovanec warned that he would just keep the items himself. He reportedly agreed to this arrangement, noting he did not want to be bothered about the boxes again.

This is not the first time Chovanec has sold items from the early life of the famous inventor. He previously auctioned off a 1977 computer poster for nearly $660,000 and a set of old bow ties that fetched over $113,000. These massive auction results highlight how collectors remain willing to spend a premium just to own a small piece of tech history, regardless of how ordinary the item might seem on the surface.

articles.title: Apple unveils M6, M5 Ultra chips and updates its desktop Macs
articles.subtitle: In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers. Both models are available to pre-order now and will ship on September 22 and will run macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Bridging the generations

The M6 chip kicks off Apple’s next chip generation, and is its first based on a 2-nanometer production process. It’s also got the first 12-core CPU in Apple’s base M-series chip line, up from 10 cores in the M4 and M5 generations.

Those CPU cores are in an interesting configuration: The M6 is the first Apple chip to mix all three of its CPU core types. The chip has six efficiency cores, four performance cores, and two super cores.

According to Apple, each core design is focused on a different primary task: efficiency cores are meant to sip power (useful when running simple background tasks); performance cores are optimized for complex, multi-threaded jobs; and super cores were created to offer the highest possible single-threaded performance.

Apple claims that this design results in record-setting single-threaded performance and up to 1.2x speed improvements over the M5 chip. The M6 also offers a dual 16-core Neural Engine, for on-device AI performance. Memory bandwidth peaks at 170GB/s, 10 percent faster than the M5.

Just as the new chip generation arrives, the previous one ( launched in October 2025 ) is completed. The M5 Ultra is Apple’s first new Ultra chip since it introduced the M3 Ultra in March 2025. Apple says it’s using the next generation of its UltraFusion technology to connect two dual-die M5 Max chips to make Apple silicon’s first quad-die chip. UltraFusion connects the two dies with bandwidth of more than 4.4TB/s, letting the four dies work as a single chip.

The M5 Ultra offers up to 36 CPU cores (12 super/24 performance), which Apple says results in up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra. It offers up to 80 GPU cores and up to 512GB of memory with 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth.

Meet the Mac mini

Previously available in M4 and M4 Pro configurations, the new Mac mini is available in M6 and M5 Pro chip options. The new base price is $899, up $100 from the previous base, for the same standard 16GB RAM/256GB storage configuration. The M5 Pro configuration starts at $1699, also up $100 from the model sold until Tuesday.

(But keep in mind, the M4 Mac mini was introduced at $599 before Apple recently raised that price. Put together, it’s a 50% price increase over the model introduced almost two years ago. We all know why, but it still hurts. )

Because the Mac mini previously shipped with M4 processors, this new model picks up numerous improvements Apple made in the M5 generation, including GPUs better optimized for AI performance. Both models support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 chip, and 2.5Gb Ethernet is now standard, with 10Gb Ethernet still available as an add-on. The M6 model supports Thunderbolt 4, but the M5 Pro model supports Thunderbolt 5.

Mac Studio advances in unison

At the same moment the Mac mini becomes split between two chip generations, the Mac Studio gets reunified with chips from the same generation: the M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. As mentioned previously, the M5 Ultra is basically two M5 Max chips connected together by Apple’s dense, fast UltraFusion technology. Apple boasts that the M5 Ultra is the fastest chip Apple has ever created, which isn’t much of a stretch since the M5 Max was already pretty far up there.

The Mac Studio is effectively the replacement for the Mac Pro, and it’s alone in offering the Ultra-class chip. Apple has positioned the Mac Studio as ideal for local AI workflows, and the new models will still be able to cluster via Thunderbolt 5 to create even larger collections of memory and performance.

Apple representatives pointed out that a four-Mac Studio AI cluster, like the one I saw on display at WWDC earlier this summer, is so efficient that it can be powered from a single standard wall outlet. (They even showed us a picture of four Mac Studios plugged into a power strip that was plugged into the wall.

) In an era of data center excesses, Apple is clearly leaning into the possibility of small, efficient Macs being used to do local AI work rather than relying on huge, power-hungry cloud models.

As with the Mac mini, the Mac Studio gains M5 chip improvements that benefit AI models running on GPU cores, integrate the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and support 2x faster storage with speeds up to 15GB/s.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: 14 years on, the creator of DayZ is still searching for a solution to survival gaming's biggest problem: 'I think I am going to die without having solved it'
articles.subtitle: "And honestly, I'm okay with that."
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
You might think making one of the most influential games of this century would be a source of unending happiness for its creator. But for Dean 'Rocket' Hall, founder of RocketWerkz, the relationship with his most famous creation isn't that simple. "When DayZ happened, it was like dying," says Hall of the mod which, alongside Minecraft, helped establish survival games as a cornerstone of the medium. "It ended my old life. My relationship with everyone who I knew up to that point changed completely."

This isn't to say Hall doesn't recognise his good fortune: "It was obviously an amazing thing that happened to me," he stresses. But there is a sense that, while Hall gained much from the creation of DayZ—fame, respect, and to a certain extent, fortune—something was lost too. "I loved making the mod, and I loved that feeling, and I've been chasing it ever since."

Chasing the feeling of making DayZ has taken over a decade, sent Hall down numerous rabbit holes and even led his studio to the precipice of bankruptcy. After all that time, Hall still hasn't found what he is looking for and admits he may never find it. Yet as he continues his search, RocketWerkz is beginning to find success on its own terms.

Hall of fame

What is it, exactly, that would rekindle the feeling of making DayZ for Hall? Specifically, he says he's searching for a solution to a specific problem he sees in survival games. "You see it time [and] again. If you go see commentary on a survival game, people will say it gets boring, or the end game sucks," he says. "And it's such a hard problem, because what you do [to] solve it [is] brute force it with heaps of content."

It's not clear when exactly Hall identified this issue, but it was likely between RocketWerkz's first and second released games. When the DayZ mod launched, Hall was working at Bohemia Interactive, the creators of ArmA 2 which served as the original basis for DayZ.

This wasn't the first mod Hall had made for ArmA 2. Indeed, it was modding that landed Hall his job at Bohemia, after his co-op mod for ArmA 2 became the most popular mod on the defunct ArmA fansite Armaholic. Despite running a major video game developer, Hall still regularly makes mods today for games like RimWorld and Barotrauma.

"People think I'm a game developer who came up from [being] a modder, and I would say I'm a modder who makes games during the day," Hall explains. "I was born a modder and I will die a modder. And I think if there's a lesson out there for any aspiring game devs, I think it's mod games. You will learn even faster than making them."

DayZ's surging popularity led Bohemia Interactive to begin creating a commercial version of the mod. Hall initially led the project, but he left Bohemia in 2014, which is when he founded RocketWerkz and began work on a project called Ion.

Ion would later be cancelled, with RocketWerkz pivoting to Stationeers, a space-station construction and management game inspired by one of Hall's favourite games, Space Station 13. Yet when it was released in 2017, Stationeers received mixed reviews, and has struggled commercially throughout its existence. "It's built up about seven years of losses," Hall says, though he adds that in 2025 it "actually probably broke even."

Close to the sun

While well received by players, Stationeers struggled commercially and remains in Steam early access. Following Stationeers, RocketWerkz began developing Icarus, a free-to-play, online survival game with a run-based loop. Players would land on a planet, go through the basic survival loop while completing an objective, launch back into space, and begin another mission that would start the cycle again.

This was Hall's attempt to solve that problem of survival games running out of road. But there were two problems. First, players didn't like the loop, as they perceived it as losing progress. "It just didn't work. People didn't want it. It was hilarious, but that's life."

Second, on launch, Icarus was not the financial success that RocketWerkz needed it to be to survive. As such, RocketWerkz pivoted quickly, abandoning the free-to-play aspect and committing to a rigorous post-launch support scheme where it would release weekly updates like clockwork. "After the beta weekend, I levelled with the team. I was like 'We do this or it's over.

' We might even do all this work and still go bankrupt, " he says. Hall is open about how gruelling a process this was. "The last couple of years, I've been enjoying it, but before that, I hated it, and we were looking at ruin, basically. "

Nonetheless, Icarus has slowly established a trusting audience, one which RocketWerkz could then sell larger, paid expansions to. "Icarus, at times, we can have a 50% attachment rate to DLC at purchase," Hall explains. "I can tell you right now, the studio would be bankrupt if we didn't do that strategy."

Yet even here, the margins can be slim. "People will go and say: 'There's too many DLC, this is crazy'. And I'll post our financials. I'll be like 'Hey, a lot of our DLC, even on Icarus— which is really good—sometimes we'll only make $100,000 from it. It might have cost us $120,000 to make. So we're not printing money."

Indeed, Hall says that it's only in the last year that Icarus has really begun making money. "We've increased our revenue 80% in the last year," he says. "Our dream for a long time has been to make more per day than we spend, because as a game developer, you need to build a big cash reserve, especially now because there's no investment money out there."

articles.title: App Report: Easy listening, easier reading
articles.subtitle: We’ve got a pair of apps that help you get a little reading done, albeit with two different approaches. Still, whether you prefer having someone else read the articles to you or if you just prefer a cleaner feed of articles, there’s something for everyone...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
We’ve got a pair of apps that help you get a little reading done, albeit with two different approaches. Still, whether you prefer having someone else read the articles to you or if you just prefer a cleaner feed of articles, there’s something for everyone in this week’s App Report.

If there’s something you think belongs in our weekly look at promising macOS and iOS apps, just drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of the app in question. We can’t reply to every email we get, but we’ll certainly take a look at any and all apps for a future column.

Listen Later

Six Colors readers may be familiar with Listen Later, which has provided a way to turn articles you’ve been meaning to read into podcasts that you can listen to at your convenience. Recently, there’s been an expansion in the ways you can access the service, with both an iOS app and a Safari extension giving you new ways to send URLs and PDFs to Listen Later so that they can be converted into a podcast.

In the iOS version of Listen Later, a Submit tab offers a field for pasting text, HTML or links; there’s also an optional button for uploading PDFs to the service. I’m able to link Listen Later to my podcatcher of choice — in this case, it’s Overcast — and a new episode featuring the content I’ve submitted shows up in my feed after it’s been converted to audio form.

The Safari extension for macOS works much the same way, only there’s a button next to the search/URL field that I tap when I want to submit something to Listen Later.

Both the Listen Later iOS app and Safari extension for macOS are free downloads, with $2 in credits for new users. If you like what you hear, you’ll need to purchase additional credits through Listen Later to cover the cost of AI processing and audio generation.

PageFeed

Reading articles on your iPhone can be a delight, but scrolling from the start of the article to the end can take some of the pleasure out of the process. If that’s a problem for you, PageFeed comes to the rescue by adopting a more book-like format for a news reader. Instead of scrolling, you tap to turn the page to make your way through an article.

The idea, PageFeed developer Brad Moss says in the description for the iOS app, is to add some degree of calm to reading through your news feed. You can select the sources and topics you want to read about. A share sheet can also send articles you find elsewhere to PageFeed for a scrolling-free experience.

You can download the app to your iPhone or iPad for free and use it for 14 days to get a feel for PageFeed’s approach. After that, a one-time $10 fee unlocks the app for good.

Tansei

It would be unfair to describe Tansei as kind of a universal clipboard for your Mac, even if that’s what this utility does, at least in a broad sense. But Tansei is really a storage space for anything. Besides text and URLs, it can hold images, screenshots and even colors, keeping them in a shelf on the side of your display for you to access whenever you need.

In my testing, Tansei has already proven its worth for a weekly newsletter I put together every week. I include a lot of links in that newsletter, and previously, that meant keeping an open text document where I could copy down URLs to articles of interest for use when it came time to put a new issue together.

With Tansei running on my Mac, all I have to do is copy the URL, and it shows up in Tansei’s shelf automatically. I can also drag-and-drop items into Tansei, and hide the app off to the side when I want an uncluttered screen.

I wish there was a way to exert a little more control over what gets copied. For example, while moving the newsletter text into the publishing site I use, every block of text I copy over appears in Tansei. At least the app offers a bulk management feature that I can use to delete unnecessary items in one fell swoop.

You can buy Tansei for a one-time payment of $7, though a three-day trial lets you use the app for free without restrictions.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: Am I out of touch? No, it's the children who are wrong: The Wii and PS3 are 'retro' now, according to iconic Japanese gaming show
articles.subtitle: 80% of nearly 17,000 viewers agree: Wii Sports is even more of a grandpa game in 2026 than it was two decades prior.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Retro gaming is just regular gaming to a sick, twisted mind like mine (and that of everyone I know, since we spend all our time playing old crap ). But what makes something retro in the first place? Is it bits? Console generation? The size and contents of the box it came in, assuming it came in one at all? Whatever it is, it seems like the Wii and PS3 are being grandfathered into the definition—at least on Game Center CX, a Japanese retro gaming TV show.

According to an article from Automaton Media, the show—which is essentially a let's play variety show starring comedian Shinya Arino—recently held a vote as to whether Wii and PS3 games should be awarded the "retro" moniker and considered for inclusion. The poll reportedly got over 14,000 responses with 71% voting in favor, and when a second round followed, that percentage rose to 80% among nearly 17,000 voters. Arino declared that games from both consoles will indeed be considered for the show moving forward.

So what does this have to do with PC gaming? Well, we have a retro gaming scene too, and if we agree for the sake of argument that those consoles are retro on the basis that they're turning 20 this year, that would mean the following PC games are also retro: Medieval II: Total War, Half-Life 2: Episode One, Dawn of War - Dark Crusade, Neverwinter Nights 2, the first season of Telltale's Sam & Max reboot, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, and perhaps most upsettingly, Company of Heroes.

Personally, I think it'd be a lot more fruitful to split our medium's history into distinct eras—something like console generations, but maybe less arbitrary than those divisions are—but it's also fun to have a label that gets thrown around once we've all agreed something is for old fuddy-duddies.

In that sense, I think the Wii and PS3 completely fit, even it's hard to swallow the notion of The Last of Us as being a game that debuted on "retro" hardware. Still, it's hard to imagine that definition will be useful for very long (if it is even of any use now). In 2046 are we going to say GTA 6 is a retro game, as if it has much of anything in common with games we hold as undeniably retro now, like Excitebike or DuckTales?

articles.title: Which Macs Will Get an M6 Chip and Which Won't?
articles.subtitle: Apple announced new Mac mini machines this week, and the lower-end models include the first M6 chip. The M6 era will be a little complicated, because few Macs are going to get it.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple announced new Mac mini machines this week, and the lower-end models include the first M6 chip. The M6 era will be a little complicated, because few Macs are going to get it. We won't have M6 Pro or M6 Max chips, which shakes up the Mac lineup for the next couple of years.

Devices With M6

The ‌Mac mini‌ is the first Mac with an M6, but the chip is going to come to a couple of other products in the lineup.

MacBook Pro - The 14-inch entry-level MacBook Pro could be updated with an M6 chip in October 2026.

iMac - The 24-inch iMac is also expected to get the M6 chip, likely around the time the ‌MacBook Pro‌ is updated.

MacBook Air - The MacBook Air could get the M6 chip in early 2027.

iPad Pro - The next iPad Pro could get the M6 chip.

iPad Air - A future version of the iPad Air is likely to adopt the M6. Apple usually keeps the ‌iPad Air‌ processor one generation behind the ‌iPad Pro‌.

M6 Pro and M6 Max

Apple isn't going to make M6 Pro or M6 Max chips, according to Bloomberg, so the M6 will be the first standalone Apple silicon chip that won't have more powerful variants.

Instead of manufacturing M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, Apple is speeding up its chip development timeline to bring the M7 Pro and M7 Max to market more quickly. The M7 Pro and M7 Max will have technologies that support on-device AI and GPU-intensive software, so they better meet growing demand for processors with those capabilities.

M5 Makes Up the Gap

Macs that would have used an M6 Pro or M6 Max chip are going to be stuck with the M5 Pro and M5 Max until the M7 family is ready. That means the high-end OLED " MacBook Ultra " we're expecting in late 2026 or early 2027 is going to use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that are in the current ‌MacBook Pro‌ models. It's also possible it will get the M5 Ultra.

The new ‌Mac mini‌ also got the M5 Pro instead of an M6 Pro chip. The new Mac Studio announced alongside the ‌Mac mini‌ uses M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips.

Short Life Span

The M6 isn't going to be around for long, because Apple plans to launch the M7 in the first half of 2027. The M7 Pro and M7 Max will follow at the end of the year.

M6 Features

The M6 is Apple's first chip built on a new 2-nanometer process that increases transistor density on a smaller die. The process change improves performance and efficiency.

articles.title: Schlage Sense Pro UWB smart lock review: What price beauty?
articles.subtitle: The Schlage Sense Pro is an unobtrusive match for my door hardware. Back in March I took possession of an Aqara UWB Smart Lock, which allowed me to live out my Star Trek dreams by using Ultra Wideband technology to sense my arrival and unlock the door without...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Back in March I took possession of an Aqara UWB Smart Lock, which allowed me to live out my Star Trek dreams by using Ultra Wideband technology to sense my arrival and unlock the door without any interaction from me. Now a second UWB lock has arrived on the scene, Schlage’s Sense Pro UWB smart lock. I’ve spent the last month locking and unlocking my front door with it, and it’s got some definite strengths over the Aqara lock—as well as some definite weaknesses.

Let’s start with the prices. The Aqara is $269, and the Schlage lock is $400. While it can be hard to justify a smart lock at any price, it’s extremely difficult to recommend one lock with much the same feature set over another when there’s this kind of price disparity.

And yes, these locks are very much playing by the same playbook: Both use UWB and Apple’s HomeKey technology to detect when your iPhone (11 or newer) or Apple Watch (Series 6 or newer) approaches your door, unlocking without having to wait or tap your device against the keypad.

You can read my previous review for more about how this works, but it’s a huge improvement on both NFC tap-to-unlock and Bluetooth proximity detection, because it can wirelessly detect if you’re inside or outside the door—and only unlocks when you’re approaching from the outside.

The Schlage Sense Pro trades versatility for compactness and attractiveness. The Aqara lock is a big black slab, compared to a relatively squat keypad that comes in either black or satin nickel (a perfect match for my front door hardware). Schlage’s lock is undeniably better looking.

It also has a light-up keypad so you can unlock it with a code, and you can program additional codes via the Schlage app or directly via the Apple Home app. And it supports NFC unlock, so if someone in your house doesn’t have a UWB device, they still have an avenue to electronically unlock the door via a tap.

Past Schlage smart locks—I used one for several years before buying the Aqara UWB model—offered a little 9-volt battery nubbin at the bottom of the outside to provide emergency power if the device’s batteries died and you needed to get into the house. This model has a USB-C port to do the same thing, and I don’t know about you, but I’m far more likely to source a USB-C cable (and an iPhone to provide power) than I am to find a 9-volt battery laying around outside my house.

Unlike the Aqara lock, the Schlage Sense Pro doesn’t have a thumbprint scanner or a physical key. The Aqara’s thumbprint scanner works but always seemed a bit pointless to me; the key, on the other hand, might have value if you like the idea of using a hide-a-key or giving a physical spare key to a friend. Alternately, it might seem unnecessary or even a security flaw. Trade-offs.

The Schlage Sense Pro is powered by four AA batteries that slide into the lock in a plastic sled; I found that if I was too forceful sliding the sled in, a battery occasionally popped out. I strongly prefer Aqara’s battery solution—a power-bank-style rechargeable battery pack that offers long life and a relatively easy USB charging path—to swapping AA batteries every so often.

My front door is not quite perfectly aligned, so automatic locks sometimes fail to lock it properly. The Schlage’s lock motor is forceful enough to do the job, but a lot less forceful than the Aqara’s, which would often have enough oomph to get the door closed even if it had to push really hard.

In truth, though, both locks were equal in their ability to lock my weird door, though Aqara is much more aggressive in making a noise when it fails to lock the door, which I appreciated more than Schlage’s somewhat muted alert.

I also appreciated Aqara’s gesture to lock the door when leaving the house—you basically tap the pad anywhere—to be a lot easier to use than the Schlage lock, which requires you tap the top portion of the touch pad twice. I got used to the double-tap, but Aqara’s was faster and less fussy.

When testing the Schlage Sense Pro, I also ran into a very odd quirk where the lock became completely unresponsive until I pulled the battery sled out and put it back in—essentially, power cycling the lock. According to Schlage, this was likely due to a faulty lock and the company supplied me with a replacement that hasn’t shown any signs of the same issue.

Both locks do a great job of unlocking automatically. This is what the whole show is really about: If I walk up to a door with my watch on my wrist or my phone in my pocket, does the door unlock by the time I put my hand on the latch? Yes, almost all the time. Very occasionally there would be a slight pause when I reached the door, but almost never.

It really is a magical feeling to have your door know that it’s you and unlock as you approach, and if you connect it to other HomeKit automations, you can have that unlock trigger other devices, like turning on your entryway lights.

In the end, the Schlage Sense Pro is a very nice lock, with a restrained look that I prefer to the Aqara’s industrial black block. Aqara’s extra locking methods (fingerprint, traditional key) are not really ones I feel are necessary. Yes, Aqara’s battery approach is better than Schlage’s, but I’ve been using AA-powered locks for ages, and it was fine, if a little annoying.

All in all, these locks are pretty close to even, with Schlage having the advantage in aesthetics. The problem is that the Schlage lock costs $130 more than the Aqara. If you don’t mind the extra charge for a more attractive lock, I won’t fault you, but for most people a smart lock is a bit of a splurge purchase as it is.

It’s not the kind of product that can be snuck by household members who are less enthusiastic about technology, and sometimes the price tag is all it takes for the household to decide that it’s not worth doing.
